subsection: 8. The impact of World War II on independent Ireland

notes.b: When war broke out in Europe in 1939, Ireland chose to stay out of it. The government called the war years the Emergency, and neutrality (staying out of a war while remaining a sovereign state) came to be seen as proof that Ireland was truly independent.
points: Fianna Fáil, led by Éamon de Valera, had been in government since March 1932, and de Valera was also Minister for External Affairs, so he personally steered Irish foreign policy as war approached.

Britain declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, and Northern Ireland, as part of the United Kingdom, was at war from that date. Partition (the division of Ireland) therefore left the island split between a belligerent and a neutral state.
The Dáil passed its emergency resolution on 2 September 1939, a day before Britain declared war, and the policy of neutrality followed from it. Do not give 3 September as the date of the resolution.
The Emergency was the official name for the war years in the South. The name let the government avoid the word war, in keeping with a policy of staying out of it.
Neutrality was formal but benevolent in practice: it leaned towards Britain and the Allies, yet it was never formally broken. Ireland was not pro-German, and it was never a member of the Allies.
notes.tip: Keep the two September dates apart: the Dáil's emergency resolution was 2 September 1939, and the Emergency Powers Act followed on 3 September. Describe neutrality as formal but benevolent, never as pro-German or pro-Allied membership.

notes.b: No single cause explains the decision. Several reasons reinforced each other, and the strongest answers rank them or link them rather than just listing them.
points: Sovereignty was the central reason: a state that followed Britain into war would look like a dominion (a self-governing state still tied to Britain) in practice, whereas staying out showed that Irish governments made their own decisions.

Partition was a second reason. Ireland could not ally with Britain while Britain held Northern Ireland, because joining Britain's war would have meant fighting beside the power that kept the island divided.

The Treaty ports (Cobh, Berehaven and Lough Swilly, naval bases Britain had kept under the 1921 Treaty) were handed back in July 1938 after the Anglo-Irish agreements of April 1938. Neutrality was therefore possible, since Britain no longer held bases on Irish soil. Churchill had opposed their return.
The Defence Forces were small and poorly equipped, and bombing of Irish cities was feared, so a state with weak defences had good reason to avoid becoming a target.

Civil War divisions were still felt, and the IRA (declared illegal in June 1936) was hostile to the government. Joining a British war might have split the country again, so neutrality helped keep national unity.

Most of the public supported neutrality, and the main parties, Fianna Fáil, Fine Gael and Labour, all accepted it. James Dillon of Fine Gael was the dissenter: in 1941 he argued for abandoning neutrality and joining the Allies.
notes.tip: Examiners ask why Ireland stayed neutral: sovereignty, partition, the ports, weak defences and Civil War divisions. Rank these or link them, for example sovereignty as the main reason and the returned ports as what made it possible, rather than just listing them.

notes.h: The Emergency Powers Act and censorship
notes.b: Once neutrality was declared, the government took wide powers over the economy and over public opinion. Control of information was meant to protect neutrality, and it also pressed the public to follow the official line.
points: The Emergency Powers Act was passed on 3 September 1939 and let ministers make orders with the force of law, without a new act of parliament each time. It covered prices, supplies, movement and censorship, and its powers continued through the war years.
Frank Aiken, Minister for the Co-ordination of Defensive Measures, ran censorship, so one minister controlled what the public could read and hear about the war.
Press censorship forbade reports on troop movements, ship sinkings, weather and criticism of neutrality. Reports that might help a belligerent (a country at war) or upset one were kept out of print.
Weather forecasts were banned from the radio and the press because they might help the belligerents, for example by guiding aircraft or ships.
Letters and telegrams were opened and censored. The Censorship of Publications Board, set up under the Censorship of Publications Act of 1929, continued to ban books during the war.
Radio Éireann (the state radio station) avoided comment that might offend any belligerent, and war news was heavily controlled.

This is conformity: state control of information that pressed the public to follow the official line. It limited press freedom and public debate, and criticism of neutrality in particular could not be published.
notes.tip: A good answer on control of opinion links the Emergency Powers Act and censorship to conformity, and notes the state's firm treatment of the IRA. For Ordinary Level, learn exactly what censorship banned: troop movements, sinkings, weather and criticism of neutrality.

notes.h: The Defence Forces, the Local Defence Force and contingency planning
notes.b: A neutral state still had to be ready to defend itself. The government greatly expanded the army and created volunteer reserves, while quietly preparing for the possibility that neutrality would fail.
points: The army was greatly expanded during the Emergency, with Reserve forces added. This was a response to the weakness of the Defence Forces and the fear of invasion or bombing.

The Local Defence Force (LDF) was founded in June 1940, after the fall of France, as a volunteer army reserve, and tens of thousands joined. The fall of France made a German invasion of Ireland seem much more likely.
The Local Security Force was a different body: it worked with the Gardaí in civil defence (protecting the civilian population). Do not confuse it with the LDF, which was a volunteer army reserve.

The government made secret contingency plans (plans for a situation that might arise) for co-operation with Britain if Germany invaded. This shows that neutrality did not mean Ireland was indifferent to who won.
notes.tip: Keep the Local Defence Force (volunteer army reserve) and the Local Security Force (civil defence with the Gardaí) apart. Say the army was greatly expanded rather than giving strength figures.

notes.b: The government saw the IRA as a threat to neutrality and to the state, because its campaign in Britain and its raids at home could draw in a belligerent. It dealt firmly with the organisation, and this firm treatment is part of the story of state control in the war years.
points: The IRA had been banned in 1936, and the Offences Against the State Act of June 1939 reinforced the law against it by giving the government powers to act against the organisation.
The IRA's S-Plan bombing campaign in Britain began in January 1939. The Coventry bomb of August 1939 killed five people, which turned British opinion against the IRA.

On 23 December 1939 the IRA raided the Magazine Fort in the Phoenix Park, Dublin, and removed the army's reserve ammunition. The government recovered most of it, but the raid showed how serious the threat was.

The Offences Against the State (Amendment) Act of 1940 introduced internment without trial (holding people without charge or court), and hundreds of IRA men were held at the Curragh. Do not confuse it with the 1939 Act, which gave powers against the IRA but not internment.
Several IRA men were executed during the war for the killing of Gardaí, and others died on hunger strike in 1940, including Tony D'Arcy and Seán McNeela.
notes.tip: Remember the difference between the two Acts: the 1939 Act gave powers against the IRA, and the 1940 Amendment Act introduced internment. A good essay on control of opinion also notes the state's firm treatment of the IRA.

notes.b: Shipping losses and British restrictions meant shortages of coal, petrol, tea and wheat. The government stepped in to control production and distribution, so that scarce goods were shared out rather than left to the market.
points: Seán Lemass was Minister for Supplies from 1939 to 1945. His Department of Supplies controlled imports, prices and rationing (limiting how much of a scarce item each person could buy), so it was the main instrument of wartime economic control.
Tea, sugar, butter, flour, bread and fuel were rationed. Petrol was restricted so tightly that private motoring almost stopped.
Compulsory tillage orders required farmers to plough more land, because imported wheat was hard to get. The wheat acreage and harvest rose, though wartime bread became darker and coarser.
Coal imports collapsed, so turf (cut and dried peat) was used as a substitute. Production grew, huge turf stacks were built in the Phoenix Park and elsewhere, and trains and homes burned turf.
Gas supplies were limited to certain hours, and inspectors, known as glimmer men, checked on households that used gas outside the permitted times.
notes.tip: Use Lemass and the Department of Supplies as specific evidence in economy answers. For Ordinary Level, learn who Lemass was, what his department did and what was rationed.

notes.h: Shipping, wages and who gained and lost
notes.b: The state had to find ships to carry the goods it needed and had to hold down wages as prices rose. The burden fell unevenly: farmers did well, while wage earners and industry suffered.
points: Irish Shipping Ltd was set up in 1941 to buy and run ships, since British shipping was unavailable. Its ships sailed unescorted under the Irish flag.
Irish merchant seamen died when ships were sunk by submarines and aircraft despite their neutral markings. Neutrality did not protect them at sea.
The Wages Standstill Order of 1941 froze most wages while prices rose, so real incomes (what wages can actually buy) fell. The Trade Union Act of 1941 was aimed at the unions.
Exports of cattle to Britain continued, and farmers gained from guaranteed prices for produce. Industry, however, suffered from lack of raw materials.
notes.tip: Better economy answers use the Wages Standstill Order as specific evidence and note who suffered (the urban poor and wage earners) and who gained (farmers).

notes.h: Relations with Britain: the 1940 offer, Churchill and the ports
notes.b: Neutrality brought repeated pressure from Britain. The pressure was sharpest in 1940, when Britain's position was at its weakest, and it continued through the battle of the Atlantic, the struggle over shipping routes in the Atlantic.
points: In June 1940, after the fall of France, Malcolm MacDonald visited Dublin and brought de Valera an offer: if Ireland joined the Allies, Britain would make a declaration in principle for a united Ireland.
De Valera declined in early July 1940. He doubted that Britain could deliver unity, and he distrusted the offer.

Churchill, who had opposed the return of the ports in 1938, publicly complained about the loss of the bases in the battle of the Atlantic, because British ships and convoys could not use them. No seizure took place.
The Irish government complained when Britain restricted supplies of coal, wheat and shipping to Ireland, since these restrictions hit the economy hard.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the 1940 unity offer (British, June to July 1940) with the American Note of 1944. For the offer, give the date, who made it, what it promised and de Valera's refusal.

notes.h: Relations with the United States and the American Note
notes.b: Once the United States joined the war, American pressure was added to British pressure. It ended in a formal request in 1944 which de Valera refused.
points: David Gray, the American Minister in Dublin (the US representative in Ireland), was strongly critical of neutrality.
The United States entered the war in December 1941 and pressed the government to give up neutrality.

On 21 February 1944 the United States, with Britain, presented the American Note, asking the government to remove the German and Japanese diplomats before the D-Day landings. This is distinct from the 1940 offer: it was American, it came in 1944, and it concerned Axis diplomats.
De Valera refused, because expelling the diplomats would have meant giving up the neutrality he had defended. Britain restricted travel to and from Ireland from February 1944.
notes.tip: For the American Note, give who presented it, the date, what it asked, that de Valera refused and what followed. A document question on the Note needs this context: what was asked, by whom, when, and de Valera's response.

notes.b: Neutrality was formal, but in practice it leaned towards Britain and the Allies. The help given was real, though it was kept quiet so that Ireland could still claim to be neutral.
points: Irish military intelligence (G2, army intelligence) co-operated with British intelligence, and the Garda watched German agents. Hermann Görtz, a German agent who parachuted into Ireland in 1940, was arrested in 1941 and interned.

Allied aircraft were allowed to fly over Donegal to the Atlantic, a route known as the Donegal air corridor, and Allied airmen who crashed in Ireland were quietly released, while Germans were interned in the Curragh.

A weather report of 3 June 1944 from Blacksod Point lighthouse, Co. Mayo, contributed to the decision to put D-Day back from 5 to 6 June 1944. This was a small but important contribution to the Allied invasion.
Tens of thousands of people from the Free State served in the British forces (estimates vary). Deserters from the Irish army who joined them were barred from state employment in 1945.
notes.tip: To show neutrality was benevolent or partial, give intelligence, the air corridor, the weather report and the release of Allied airmen. Linking this to pressure from Churchill and the United States gives a balanced answer.

notes.h: German bombing and aid to Belfast
notes.b: Neutrality did not keep Irish towns safe from German aircraft. Bombs fell on the South in 1940 and 1941, although the Irish government still sent help north when Belfast was bombed.
points: German aircraft bombed the creamery at Campile, Co. Wexford, on 26 August 1940, and three people were killed. Other places were also bombed.
On the night of 31 May 1941 German bombers dropped bombs on the North Strand in Dublin, killing about 30 people (counts range from 28 to 34) and destroying or damaging many houses.
The government protested to Germany, and Germany said it was an error. West Germany paid compensation after the war.

Fire brigades from Dublin and other towns went north to help Belfast in April 1941, with the approval of de Valera. The Belfast blitz was the bombing of Northern Ireland, and the North Strand raid, in contrast, was a German error in a neutral state.
notes.tip: Keep the North Strand bombing (Dublin, 31 May 1941, an error) apart from the Belfast blitz (Northern Ireland). Give the date and the range of casualty figures (28 to 34) rather than a single exact count.

notes.h: The end of the war: Hitler's death and the Churchill exchange
notes.b: De Valera's insistence on diplomatic correctness (following proper diplomatic form) to the end brought a public attack from Churchill, and de Valera's reply became one of the best-known statements of Irish neutrality.
points: On 2 May 1945, after Hitler's death was announced, de Valera called on the German minister, Eduard Hempel, to express condolences.

He had made a similar call on Gray, the American Minister, after Roosevelt's death in April 1945. This is why he defended the visit as diplomatic protocol that a neutral state had followed throughout the war.
Many Irish and Allied commentators criticised the visit to Hempel, because it came as the full horror of the Nazi regime was becoming known.
In his victory broadcast of 13 May 1945 Churchill attacked Irish neutrality and referred to the ports.
De Valera replied on Radio Éireann on 16 May 1945. He argued that Churchill had shown how a great power might justify interfering with the rights of a small state, and that Ireland had stood alone.
The broadcast was widely praised in Ireland and strengthened de Valera's reputation, though it did not improve relations with Britain.
notes.tip: Learn the dates: Hempel visit on 2 May 1945, Churchill's broadcast on 13 May and de Valera's reply on 16 May. Explain why he made the call, which was protocol, and note the similar visit on Roosevelt's death.

notes.b: The war closed many routes abroad and imposed austerity at home, but the British labour market opened up. Those who stayed faced hardship, and the first steps in social policy came late in the period.
points: Tens of thousands of workers went to Britain during the war to work in factories and construction, and sent money home (remittances), which helped families who stayed in Ireland.
The Irish economy suffered from shortages, and unemployment remained high for those who stayed, which is why emigration to British war work attracted so many.
Prices rose faster than wages, so the poor in Dublin and other towns suffered most.
The government used its emergency powers to maintain control of the press and labour, and there was little organised protest.
The Children's Allowances Act of 1944 and the creation of a separate Department of Health in 1947 were the first steps in post-war social policy.
Many Irish women and men served in the British forces, and the Irish government gave them little recognition after the war.
notes.tip: In society answers, name who suffered (the urban poor, wage earners) and who gained (farmers), and use emigration and rationing as dated or specific evidence.

notes.b: Judgements depend on whether the priority is sovereignty and survival or the moral and economic costs. Strong answers argue that neutrality kept independence, but at a heavy cost.
points: Achievement: the state avoided invasion and bombing on the scale of Belfast and kept its independence, so neutrality delivered the sovereignty it was meant to protect.
Achievement: neutrality was popular and strengthened national unity after the Civil War.
Limit: shortages, wage controls and censorship reduced living standards and freedom of expression.
Limit: the policy isolated Ireland from the Allies and left it without a voice at the end of the war.
Contemporary view: supporters called it a principled defence of independence, while critics said it was selfish, as Churchill suggested.

Later view: historians such as J. J. Lee (Ireland 1912-1985) and Brian Girvin (The Emergency, 2006) stress the practical advantages of neutrality and its pro-Allied bias, but also question the moral cost. Robert Fisk (In Time of War, 1983) was critical.
notes.tip: The commonest Higher essay sets the impact of the war on both parts of Ireland against each other. For the South, argue a clear thesis that neutrality kept independence but at a heavy cost, show political, economic and social effects each with a dated example, and name a historian such as Lee or Girvin.

keyTerms.definition: The policy of staying out of the war, adopted on 3 September 1939 as a demonstration of Irish sovereignty.
The official Irish name for the Second World War period, during which special powers applied.
The 1939 Act giving ministers power to make orders with legal force over the economy, movement and censorship.
Government control of the press, radio, letters and books during the Emergency, run through Frank Aiken's department.
The pressure on citizens and media to follow the official line, strengthened by wartime censorship.
The part-time volunteer reserve founded in June 1940 to support the army.
The department under Lemass that controlled imports, prices and rationing during the war.
The state shipping company set up in 1941 to carry essential cargoes.
The request of February 1944 that Ireland expel Axis diplomats, which de Valera refused.
Detention without trial, used against the IRA at the Curragh under the 1940 Act.
